CHIEF COMPLAINT
Big toe pain and redness.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient reports pain in big toe that has been present off and on for about two weeks, with significant worsening last week. Patient was at a trade show/convention where he could not walk the halls and had to remain standing due to severe pain. Patient describes the pain as throbbing in nature but occasionally sharp and stabbing, especially with movement or prolonged walking. Patient notes he walks on his heel to avoid bending the toe. Pain is exacerbated by light pressure, such as bed sheets at night. Patient denies any remembered injury but became concerned when the toe became red and warm to touch. Patient reports taking 2 ibuprofen daily without significant relief.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Patient denies stomach problems. Reports loving hot Mexican food.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Not discussed.

MEDICATIONS
Ibuprofen 2 tablets daily.

ALLERGIES
Not discussed.

FAMILY HISTORY
Not discussed.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient works on his feet daily. Loves to ride bikes on trails, has put in over 800 miles on trails in the last year, pedals with back of feet in regular shoes or flip flops. Loves to fish.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Big toe examination reveals redness and warmth. Range of motion testing shows pain with dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, with approximately 10 degrees of plantarflexion causing pain and 20 degrees causing increased pain. Medial-lateral movement elicits pain with grinding sensation noted. Palpation between big toe and second toe causes mild discomfort. Palpation on lateral side of toe causes significant discomfort. Bone spur palpated on top of big toe joint.

RESULTS
X-ray of big toe shows large spur on top of big toe joint with significant loss of cartilage consistent with arthritis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Hallux rigidus with arthritic changes. Patient to be fitted with orthotic insert for shoe. Start meloxicam once daily for anti-inflammatory effect; patient to stop and call if develops heartburn or pain below sternum. Patient to continue regular work and activities. Follow-up appointment in two weeks to assess response to treatment. If no significant improvement noted, will consider injection, arthroscopic joint cleaning, or joint fusion depending on severity.
